title: Coherent extrapolated volition
summary:
Coherent Extrapolated Volition (CEV) is a concept in AI alignment proposed by Eliezer Yudkowsky in 2004. CEV proposes that an advanced AI system should derive its goals by extrapolating the idealized volition of humanity, meaning it would aggregate and project human preferences into a coherent utility function reflecting what people would desire under ideal epistemic and moral conditions.

According to Yudkowsky and Nick Bostrom, CEV has several interesting properties. It is designed to be humane and self-correcting, by capturing the source of human values instead of trying to list them, thus avoiding the difficulty of laying down an explicit, fixed list of rules. It encapsulates moral growth, preventing flawed current moral beliefs from getting locked in. It limits the influence that a small group of programmers can have on what the ASI would value, thus also reducing the incentives to build ASI first.

A philosophical analysis explored CEV through the lens of social trust in autonomous systems, proposing an evolution into "Coherent, Extrapolated and Clustered Volition" (CECV), which aims to better reflect the moral preferences of diverse cultural groups.

Almost immediately after publishing the idea in 2004, Yudkowsky himself described the concept as outdated and warned against conflating it with a practical strategy for AI alignment. In Nick Bostrom's Superintelligence, he explores how we might design AI systems to discover and align with moral truths or human values without directly specifying them, through strategies of indirect normativity, with CEV being one such approach.
